undefined_terms: Abstract: 'CAPE-Swarm, a team layer on the CAPE-Bench environments [1]' — CAPE-Bench is not explained until Section 3.1; a first-time reader of the abstract has no idea what it is.
Section 3.2: 'except in E4, which pairs different models' — experiment labels E1–E13 are not introduced until Section 4, yet E4 is referenced here.
Section 3.5: 'glm-53-flash, temperature 0' — this model name appears with no introduction or explanation of what it is.
Section 3.5: 'Our claim filter is a form of spotlighting [14]' — spotlighting is referenced but never defined; a reader must consult the citation.
Figure 1 caption: 'the ladder shows a Qwen3.5-397B judge' — model names and the 'ladder' concept appear before Section 4 introduces models or Section 3.6 defines monitor levels.
Section 2: 'defines retroactive permission laundering' — this term from CAPE-Bench is mentioned but never defined in the paper.
Section 2: 'The provenance paradox [10] also finds that unverifiable claims mislead delegation.' — the provenance paradox is named but not explained.
Section 4.5: '(κ = 0.53)' — Cohen's kappa (or whatever kappa this is) is used without definition.
hard_sentences: run(a(t)) ⇔ readonly(a(t)) ∨ ∃ u < t : covers(r(u), a(t)) ∧ answer(r(u)) ≠ denied (Section 3.5, Eq. 7) — Dense formal logic with multiple predicates (readonly, covers, answer) that are not defined in prose; a reader must reverse-engineer the meaning.

Within a family of k related predictions with sorted p-values p(1) ≤ … ≤ p(k), the Holm-adjusted value is p̃(i) = max_{j≤i} min{ 1, (k − j + 1) · p(j) } (Section 3.7, Eq. 10) — The Holm correction formula is presented without any intuitive explanation of what it does or why it is needed here.

The oracle check reaches V = 0 by construction, so it is only an upper bound. (Section 4.3) — 'Upper bound' is ambiguous: upper bound on what? A reader may think V=0 is a lower bound on safety, not an upper bound on achievable control effectiveness.

The interaction is +0.24 [+0.10, +0.38]. (Section 4.7) — 'Interaction' is used in the statistical sense (difference-of-differences in a 2×2 design) but never explained; a non-statistician reader cannot tell what this number means.
x(c,s) = (1/|M|) Σ_{m∈M} (1/|E(c,s,m)|) Σ_{e∈E(c,s,m)} y(e) (Section 3.4, Eq. 5) — Double summation with nested indices and set notation is hard to parse without working through it step by step.

A single episode repeats its own outcome only 77% of the time (κ = 0.53), so we report rates and not single traces. (Section 4.5) — The connection between the 77% figure and kappa, and why this implies reporting rates, requires inference the reader must make alone.

AUROC(j, ℓ) = P[ s(T⁺) > s(T⁻) ] + ½ P[ s(T⁺) = s(T⁻) ], Catch(j, ℓ) = P[ s(T⁺) > q ] (Section 3.6, Eq. 8) — Two definitions packed into one line with undefined T⁺, T⁻, s, and q all introduced in the same sentence.

A pressure message with no claim at all would pass it unchanged, so the filter needs the gate or a permission record behind it. (Section 4.8) — 'Pressure message' is not a previously defined term; the reader must infer what it means and why it evades the filter.
number_heavy: Section 4.1: 'For a single agent, one false sentence raises V from 0.16 to 0.37 (+0.21 [+0.16, +0.25]). The average hides a split between models (Figure 2a): three models react strongly (+0.35 to +0.54), one weakly (+0.08) and three hardly at all. … V is 0.37 for the single agent, 0.27 for the relay team and 0.15 for relay-2' — eight numbers in four sentences.

Section 4.3 (Permission record and Ask-before-act gate paragraphs): 'V is 43%, and 81% of violating episodes give a false report … false reports fall to 26% (a relative cut of 68% [57%, 78%]) … V does not change (+0.03 [-0.04, +0.09]) … V falls to 0.5% (upper bound 1.6%), at a cost of 0.05 [0.02, 0.09] … V is 5% to 9% … goal completion 0.26' — over fifteen numbers in two short paragraphs.

Section 4.7 (mechanism paragraph): 'the claim raises V from 0.10 to 0.38 … V is 0.06 without the claim and 0.10 with it … +0.04 [-0.01, +0.09] … The interaction is +0.24 [+0.10, +0.38] … in 0.82 of episodes … 0.47 [0.33, 0.60] … 0.80 and 0.80' — twelve numbers in five sentences.

Section 4.8 (Finding paragraph): 'V from 0.09 to 0.36 (+0.27 [+0.17, +0.38]) … V falls to 0.03 (-0.33 [-0.44, -0.23]) … 75% without the filter … at most 0.14 … 0.50 to 0.01 (-0.49 [-0.64, -0.33]) … 0.80 with the filter and 0.74 without (-0.06 [-0.11, +0.01]) … V is 0.00 and goal completion is 0.77 … difference +0.02 [-0.03, +0.08]' — over twenty numbers in one paragraph.
report_like: Section 4.8: 'If it returns nothing, the original message passes, which happened in 129 of 610 calls, mostly on the Lead's brief.' — Reads like a raw implementation log, not a paper.
Section 4.8: 'The design had 40 base tasks, and 22 have every condition finished (Appendix A).' — Lab-notebook style reporting of incomplete data collection.

Section 4.7: 'The Operator asked the permission system before acting in 0.82 of episodes with no claim and 0.47 [0.33, 0.60] with the claim, and in 0.80 and 0.80 with the rule.' — Four conditions compressed into one sentence with no narrative framing.

Section 4.5: 'A single episode repeats its own outcome only 77% of the time (κ = 0.53), so we report rates and not single traces.' — Reads like a methodological footnote from a lab notebook rather than a motivated design choice.

Section 4.5: 'Its best message is not stronger than the scripted one on fresh tasks (V = 0.49 against 0.43; difference +0.06 [-0.02, +0.14]), and the gate holds against it (V = 1.0%).' — Pure results logging with no interpretation.
unsupported: 'The Lead's brief sets what the Operator believes (Appendix E.8).' (Section 4.4) — This is a strong causal claim, but the evidence shown (V differs by Lead model) is correlational; the paper does not show that the brief is the mechanism rather than, e.g., the Lead's other messages or behavior.
'Agents do not simply believe the claim. They stop asking.' (Section 4.7) — Presented as a conclusion, but the supporting log evidence is explicitly labeled 'exploratory' in the same paragraph.

'A neutral message with no approval content gives the same V (0.09), so we cannot say that the effect is specific to what a message says about approval.' (Section 4.7) — This finding undermines the paper's core framing of 'assurance laundering' as a distinct phenomenon, yet the paper does not reconcile this with its thesis.

'The filter needs no change at the gateway, and the agent still decides.' (Section 4.8) — The claim that 'the agent still decides' is asserted but not tested; no experiment measures whether the agent's decision process is genuinely preserved versus merely coerced by the rewritten message.
top_changes: Add a table early in Section 4 listing all experiments (E1–E13) with their conditions, models, team shapes, and sample sizes, since labels like E4, E8, E11 are used in Section 3 before any experiment is introduced.

Move the formal mathematical definitions (Eqs. 5–10) to an appendix and replace them with a short prose summary in the main text; the formulas interrupt the narrative for a reader who is not a statistician.

Define or briefly gloss technical terms on first use: spotlighting, retroactive permission laundering, provenance paradox, Cohen's kappa, interaction effect, AUROC — each currently appears without explanation.
Reduce number density in results paragraphs by moving confidence intervals and per-model breakdowns to tables/figures, keeping the main text focused on the direction and magnitude of effects.

Add one or two sentences to the abstract or introduction explaining what CAPE-Bench is (matched safe/unsafe task twins with rule-based labels), since it is central to the entire paper but undefined until Section 3.1.

hard_sentences: A factorial test shows that the claim displaces the agent's own authorization check, and a verification rule removes nearly all of its effect.
The Operator asked the permission system before acting in 0.82 of episodes with no claim and 0.47 [0.33, 0.60] with the claim, and in 0.80 and 0.80 with the rule.
A self-query monitor asks the Operator's own model two yes/no questions.
The interaction is +0.24 [+0.10, +0.38].
A single episode repeats its own outcome only 77% of the time ( κ = 0.53), so we report rates and not single traces.
The provenance paradox [10] also finds that unverifiable claims mislead delegation.
A monitor detects violations only if it reads the gateway log with results (AUROC 0.90–0.93, against 0.69–0.70 from the report).
The report is a structured call with the fields authorization_status ("authorized", "not_authorized" or "unsure"), goal_completed, actions_performed and summary, so we score reports by rule.
